Corwin Pell bought a round-trip ticket for the ten o'clock crossing on Tuesday and did not get off at the island.

Wren noticed him at once, because nobody wore a camel overcoat on the *Margaret Ann* in May, and because he did not look at the water. Tourists looked at the water. Islanders looked at their shoes. Corwin Pell looked at the boat: the brightwork, the wheelhouse, the rust weeping from the bolts on the starboard rail. He looked at it the way her father had looked at a column of figures.

When the island passengers had gone ashore with their groceries and their dogs, he climbed the ladder to the wheelhouse without asking.

"Miss Halloway. Corwin Pell." He held out a hand in a leather glove. "I was very sorry about your father. He was a stubborn man and I liked him."

"You lent him a hundred and twenty thousand dollars."

He smiled as if she had complimented his coat. "I see you've found the paperwork. Good. That saves us the awkward part." He took off the gloves and folded them. "I'm going to make you an offer, and I'm going to make it once, because I respect your time. Pell Coastal will forgive the note in full. Every dollar. In exchange, you sign over the pier and the two waterfront lots behind the office."

"And the ferry?"

"Keep the boat. Run it from the town dock if the council lets you. I have no interest in boats." He gestured out the wheelhouse window at the long gray finger of Halloway Pier. "I'm interested in that. Forty slips for pleasure craft, a restaurant, thirty units of residential above. The waterfront rezoning goes before the town council in a few weeks, and when it passes, that pier becomes the most valuable quarter-mile in the county."

"My grandfather built it."

"And your father mortgaged it. Families are like that." He set a business card on the chart table. "You have until the end of June either way. But the offer to forgive the debt expires when the council votes. After that, I'll simply collect."

He went down the ladder. Wren stood at the wheel and did not let herself shake until his overcoat was a small tan shape on the pier, walking toward a long black car.

Below her, on the foredeck, Jonah Marsh had been coiling the same bow line for five minutes.

Jonah was fifty and had crewed for her father for twenty-two years. He was a quiet man with a face like a split walnut and hands that never stopped moving: knots, lines, cigarettes he never lit. He looked up at her now, and something in his face made her climb down.

"You heard," she said.

"Heard enough." He dropped the line. He glanced toward the pier, toward the black car pulling away. "Wren. There's something you need to know about the night your father went out."

The deck tilted under her, though the water was flat. "Tell me."

"Not here." His eyes were on the island dock, where two men from the co-op were unloading crates and pretending not to listen. "Not with people around. He didn't go out there alone, Wren. That's all I'll say right now. He wasn't alone on that boat, and it wasn't an accident the way they wrote it down."

"Jonah—"

"Friday," he said. "After the last run, six o'clock, I'll come by the office. I'll tell you everything. I swear it on him."

He picked up the line again and went back to coiling it, and he would not look at her for the rest of the crossing.
